source.title_on_document: Borrowed or kept? How self-generation-first and direct-adoption AI workflows shape immediate unaided reasoning

supplement.where: The document refers to no supplementary file or online appendix. Instruction scripts, system prompt, prompt-template pool, model version, writing prompts, rating rubric, and de-identified data are 'available from the corresponding authors upon reasonable request' (p. 5, Section 2.5; p. 13, Data availability statement).
supplement.holds: Nothing identified. Arm-level unadjusted means and SDs of the outcomes are not printed anywhere in this PDF.

paper_design_summary: Adults recruited on an online research platform (Chinese-speaking students and early-career workers) were randomized to write a 300-500 word argumentative essay (Phase 1) under one of three conditions: an autonomous workflow (own thesis and outline required before the Qwen3.5 AI panel unlocked, then compare and rewrite), a dependent workflow (generate the essay with AI and adopt its output with minimal change), or no AI. About 15-20 minutes later, in the same session, all participants wrote a parallel argumentative essay on a different policy topic with no AI available (Phase 2). Two blind raters scored each essay on 1-7 rubrics for reasoning quality (primary), idea diversity (number and breadth of distinct perspectives within the essay), and originality (novelty relative to templated answers).

studies.label: Three-arm workflow experiment (argumentative essay with or without AI, then unaided parallel essay)

assignment.what_was_assigned: AI workflow for the Phase-1 essay: autonomous (self-generation-first) AI workflow, dependent (direct-adoption) AI workflow, or no AI
assignment.quote: Participants were assigned by stratified block randomization (strata: baseline-ability tertile crossed with student or worker status; block size six; equal allocation), with the assignment sequence generated and recorded by the online system.
assignment.locator: p. 6, Section 2.8; also p. 3, Section 2.1 (single-factor, three-level between-subjects design) and p. 4, Table 2 (Randomized row)
assignment.prereg_locator: p. 3, Section 2.1.1: 'The study was not formally preregistered'; primary endpoint, covariates, exclusion criteria, and BH family were fixed in a dated internal analysis plan written before the data were analyzed

arms.name: Autonomous
arms.description: Self-generation-first workflow: interface step-lock required a written position and a 3-5 point outline (at least 80 characters) before the AI panel opened; then a comparison box required recording at least one disagreement with the AI's points and judging which side was better founded; final text had to be rewritten in the participant's own words.

arms.name: Dependent
arms.description: Direct-adoption workflow: no outline step; instructed 'Use AI to complete this argumentative essay... adopt the AI output as it stands, with minimal changes.'

arms.name: No-AI
arms.description: Wrote the Phase-1 essay independently; prohibited from using any AI tool, search engine, or external material.

participants.exclusions: 241 of 900 randomized were excluded after assignment (Table 2): failed an attention check (29/31/29 autonomous/dependent/no-AI; 89 total), did not complete Phase 2 (26/39/30; 95 total), long-string responding (4/2/4; 10 total), and flagged by a research-team AI-authorship screen in the no-AI arm only (69). Categories overlap. Exclusions per arm 56/69/116 (20.1%, 23.5%, 35.4%; chi2(2) = 20.22, p < 0.0001). Paper calls the 659-person analysis modified intention-to-treat. Sensitivity samples: per-protocol n = 585 (172/201/212); all randomized with a Phase-2 essay n = 805; multiple imputation over all 900 (Table 4).
participants.who: Adults who reported using generative AI for cognitive tasks, recruited through an online research participant platform with quotas across student and early-career-worker status; mean age 24.6, 54% women
participants.country: Not stated explicitly; participants described as Chinese-speaking students and early-career workers recruited online (p. 13), with a Chinese-language writing assistant and a Chinese university ethics approval
participants.quote: Of 900 participants who began the study, we excluded those who failed either attention check (89), did not complete the Phase-2 task (95), showed indications of AI use in the no-AI condition (69; see below), or produced long-string responding (10)

ai_tool.name_model: Qwen3.5 (Tongyi Qianwen; Alibaba Cloud), called through the official API with one pinned version and fixed sampling parameters; identical system prompt in both AI arms casting it as a general-purpose Chinese-language writing assistant
ai_tool.how_used: AI served through the study platform's AI panel, not a public chatbot; calls per participant not capped (observed 1-8, median 3). Both AI arms used the same model and prompt-template pool; the arms differed only in the interface workflow (step-lock and compare/rewrite in autonomous; direct generation and adoption in dependent). Autonomous participants adopted a mean of 32% of AI content without rewriting vs 73% in the dependent arm (p. 7, Section 3.1). AI available only in Phase 1.

task.description: Argumentative essays on public-policy questions: Topic A (ban private cars from city centers) and Topic B (move from a 5-day to a 4-day work week), counterbalanced across phases. Phase 1: AI-assisted (or unaided in no-AI arm) essay of 300-500 words. Phase 2: structurally parallel essay of 300-500 words with no AI for any arm. A short unaided baseline essay (homework policy, 120-200 words, 5-7 min) before randomization served as a covariate.
task.duration: Phase 1: 12-15 min limit; Phase 2: 10-12 min limit, 15-20 min after Phase 1 in the same session; baseline essay 5-7 min (p. 5, Sections 2.3 and 2.5). Observed mean Phase-1 time 14.2/13.1/13.3 min and Phase-2 time 11.3/11.8/11.5 min (Table 1).

outcomes.name: Phase-2 (unaided) reasoning quality
outcomes.question: after_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: 1-7 rubric with defined anchors: clarity of thesis, relevance and sufficiency of evidence, coherence of reasoning, handling of counterarguments. Two raters blind to condition and phase (credentials not stated), calibrated to ICC(2,k) >= 0.75; third rater for disagreements of 2+ points; rater mean used. Phase-2 ICC(2,k) = 0.86. ANCOVA adjusting for baseline writing ability and Phase-2 time on task, no-AI reference. Coded as usefulness (quality of a single output); it is not a creativity rating. Robustness variants: per-protocol, HC3, single-rater scores, Phase-1 time/effort/performance adjustments, relaxed exclusions, multiple imputation, time floors (Table 4, p. 10); change from baseline essay (no-AI -0.02, autonomous +0.17, dependent -0.49; F(2, 656) = 15.66, p < 0.0001; p. 12).

eligibility.reason: Individuals were randomized (stratified block randomization, p. 6) to two generative-AI workflows or a no-AI control for an essay task; 659 people analyzed (900 randomized; p. 3-4). Blind raters scored the essays on originality and idea diversity as well as reasoning quality, both while AI was available (Phase 1, autonomous vs dependent only) and 15-20 min after AI was removed (Phase 2, all three arms). Boundary note: the task is argumentative writing and the paper's primary outcome is reasoning quality; the creativity-related outcomes (originality, within-essay idea diversity) are secondary. Large post-randomization exclusions (241 of 900, uneven by arm because of a no-AI-only AI-use screen).

one_line_finding: In the unaided Phase-2 essay, the dependent-AI arm scored below the no-AI arm on reasoning quality (-0.38, 95% CI [-0.59, -0.18], d = -0.28) and idea diversity (-0.30, d = -0.23) but not on originality (-0.07, d = -0.02, q = 0.28), while the autonomous arm did not fall below no-AI (p. 7-8, Section 3.4 and Figure 2).
open_questions: Whether an argumentative essay scored on originality and within-essay idea diversity counts as a creative task under the codebook ('essays judged for creativity'); reasoning quality, the primary outcome, is not a creativity rating.
Reasoning quality coded as usefulness (quality of a single output); reviewers may prefer other.

Idea diversity is a within-essay rating of distinct perspectives and is coded flexibility; the paper reports no cross-participant diversity or similarity measure, so there is no across_people outcome.
Rater background is not stated (coded human_raters rather than expert_raters).
The 69 no-AI exclusions rest on a single team judgment of AI authorship with no reliability statistic; the paper reports the primary contrast with them restored (-0.38, n = 713, Table 4).

Two AI arms share the no-AI control; under codebook rule 8.3 the primary after_ai record would use the arm closest to free chatbot use (likely Dependent), but the dependent arm is an instructed adoption extreme, not free use.
notes: Page numbers are the PDF pages, which match the printed page numbers (01-15). The paper prints no unadjusted arm means or SDs for the outcomes; Figure 2A shows covariate-adjusted means with +/-1 SE bars only graphically. Phase-1 contrasts against no-AI are not reported. Section 2.8 states achieved cells of '209-225 per arm' while Table 2 gives 212-225; I record the Table 2 counts. Trait (ACO) hierarchical regressions, mediation through metacognitive monitoring and intrinsic motivation, and process-log associations (Sections 3.8-3.10) are not contrasts between assigned arms on a creativity outcome and are not listed as outcomes. Phase-1 time differed by arm (autonomous 14.2 vs dependent 13.1 min); adjusting for it leaves the primary contrast at -0.39 (Table 4).
